Senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, arrival within integration (兼中到) is the fifth named relation. Dongshan’s verse places it outside the opposition of existence and nonexistence; later records repeatedly describe distinctions as exhausted or integrated. Dongshan Liangjie begins the fifth-rank verse by saying it falls into neither existence nor nonexistence. Hongzhi Zhengjue gives it a dawn verse, while an unnamed monastic asks Fenyang Shanzhao for it and receives images of a weaving jade woman and a drumming stone man. Langting Ting uses a returning cuckoo, Juelang Daosheng offers a later black-white diagram, Yongjue Yuanxian says affairs and principle are both gone, and Ruibai Mingxue applies it to a shout after holy and ordinary, subject and object, and existence and nonexistence are exhausted. These remain attributed illustrations of one rank.

Senses.Explanation: To make something clear or bring it to light. Chan biographies repeatedly say that someone brings “the great matter,” “the mind-ground,” or “the essentials of mind” to light. One record lists bringing the great matter to light alongside having one's mind-ground opened through mountains and waters and recognizing one's original face through things encountered; the text supplies these neighboring predicates without making them synonyms. A later address states its aim as having each person “directly bring to light one's own fundamental great matter” (直下發明自己本分大事), anchoring direct instruction rather than retrospective biography. Other biographies say “there will certainly be clarification” (必有發明) or that someone was “not greatly clarified” (不大發明). Those result and degree constructions name the outcome of the same bringing-to-light event, not another lexical referent.

Senses.Explanation: To swear an oath is to make an explicit pledge; the surviving witnesses record different oath contents and do not all describe a public performance. The Xuefeng Genxin row is compiler biography: it says he vowed to travel and then went to Gushan, not that he utters the headword. Another biography records a private vow to travel to China, a training text says one must vow in order to endure discipline, and Baozhi recalls a vow made with an Indian monk. The common element is an explicit pledge, while publicity is not established as defining.
